name: Polypogon

project_scope.scope: Existing canonical species only; no new admission

look_here_first: ANNUAL BEARDGRASS / RABBIT'S-FOOT GRASS: in damp ditches and disturbed soils look for a short-to-medium ANNUAL grass with a dense, soft, pale-green to tawny cylindrical or lobed flowerhead. The fluffy HALO comes chiefly from TWO long awns (typically 4–10 mm) arising from notched tips of the TWO GLUMES around each tiny one-flowered spikelet. The much smaller fertile lemma can ALSO bear a short awn: NEVER teach 'glumes awned, lemma always awnless.' Separate introduced Setaria by bristle origin (sterile branchlets beneath spikelets), and Carolina Phalaris by compact firm glumes without this long awn halo.

comparison_lesson.title: Soft rabbit-foot beardgrass versus canarygrass, foxtail and water bentgrass
comparison_lesson.memory_rule: POLYPOGON = TWO LONG AWNED GLUMES per one-flowered spikelet + SHORT lemma (sometimes ALSO short-awned). SETARIA = bristles beneath spikelets from sterile branches. PHALARIS = broader firm glumes, no rabbit-foot fuzz.
quick_split: Polypogon monspeliensis: tiny single-flowered spikelet with 2 notched GLUMES each bearing very long hairlike awn (4–10 mm); short lemma may also have short awn.
Phalaris caroliniana: densely layered pointed broad keeled glumes, no outward furry glume-awn halo; requires reduced sterile floret dissection for exact Phalaris species.
Setaria spp.: visible bristles are sterile BRANCHLETS below spikelets, not elongated awns on paired glumes; ligule usually hair fringe not membranous.
Polypogon viridis: glumes not conspicuously long-awned, creeping perennial; green dense head may resemble annual beardgrass if awns not inspected.
Phleum pratense and Alopecurus: other foxtail-shaped grasses; inspect glume awns vs lemma awns and spikelet count with magnification.
comparison_lesson.guardrail: Do not invent precise awn insertion in un-dissected photo, or certify Hays nativity. All additional taxa comparison-only, no new species admission.

comparison_matrix.title: Fuzzy grass heads — WHAT bears the bristles?
rows: Very soft fuzzy green/straw cylinder or lobed head, wet disturbed ground
Two GLUMES each tipped with one long 4–10 mm awn from a shallow notch; lemma very short, often separately short-awned; annual
Green contracted head, often creeping stems
Glumes AWNLESS; often perennial, rooting at nodes
Compact firm overlapping seedhead, pointed glumes
Broad, keeled glumes, no many fine long glume awns; two reduced sterile florets in mature dissection
Foxtail bristle halo on dense head
Bristles BELOW spikelets are sterile branches, NOT glume awns; hair-fringed ligule
Glume awns much shorter, lemmas unawned; different glume keel hairs
Usually lemma awns rather than two long prominent paired glume awns; verify actual spikelet anatomy

what_to_teach_crew: FIRST—head: softly fuzzy or rabbit-foot-like compact green to straw-colored narrowly ellipsoid/cylindrical panicle; sometimes branched lobes, not necessarily one uniform straight cylinder.
SECOND—annual base: tufted/ascending slender culms with fibrous roots, often in moist soil; do not infer rooted annual anatomy from cropped seedhead photos.

THIRD—one ACTUAL mature spikelet at 10–20×: TWO narrow glumes, each with a notch and a long slender awn from the notch, usually 4–10 mm. Hair/awn origin must be traced from the base, not guessed from the outside halo.

FOURTH—inside those glumes: ONE fertile floret; the much shorter shiny lemma often has its own much shorter awn, sometimes apparently awnless depending on specimen; never call the long outer hair a lemma awn from the group photo.
FIFTH—true leaf collar: a translucent MEMBRANOUS ligule typically several mm long, not a Setaria hair-fringed ligule; capture a scaled true sheath/blade junction.

SIXTH—check introduced look-alikes: P. viridis (generally awnless glumes and creeping/perennial), Setaria spp. (bristles from sterile branches rather than two paired glumes), Phleum pratense (shorter glume awns), Phalaris caroliniana (firm broad keeled scales, no long fuzzy halo) and Alopecurus spp. (shorter/absent glume awns; often lemma-awns).

items.label: ANNUAL BEARDGRASS — Texas macro of fuzzy glume-awn halo
items.image_role: Publicly licensed exact photo from North Texas of an awned contracted green head; visible head and awn halo only, NO split-glume notch at millimeter scale.
items.caption: Annika Lindqvist's Texas photograph makes the many pale hairlike projections around this green, occasionally interrupted cylindrical head obvious. These are the GLUME AWNS responsible for the fuzzy appearance, but the precise junction of an awn with an individual split glume is NOT resolved here. The site was North Texas, not a Hays specimen.
items.why_it_matters: Shows real fine awns and the strongly contracted panicle, allowing a crew member to distinguish a soft beardgrass from firm overlapping Phalaris canarygrass.
items.creator: Annika Lindqvist
